clue.text: Keep hoping undraped women at the end smile mischievously

indicators.note: acting mischievously means playing tricks and causing disorder, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone clings to the hope of a glimpse of naked women, grinning naughtily the whole time.
explanation.walkthrough: NIL DESPERANDUM is a Latin motto, 'never despair', so the definition is an imperative. 'Undraped' and 'smile' are fodder hiding in plain sight among the cheeky picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin tag tells a person never to give up and to stay optimistic, which is an instruction to carry on with hope.

clue.text: Negotiate in war shamefully showing disrespect?

indicators.note: doing something shamefully means doing it badly and improperly, so the letters are put together wrongly

parts.note: the letters of these three words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A diplomat conducts peace talks in wartime in a way that insults the other side.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: turning up open-collared at a formal occasion can be read as a lack of respect.
explanation.definitionFit: Going without formal neckwear where dress codes expect it is taken as a slight, so the phrase is an example of discourtesy.

clue.text: What am I doing, increase in size permitting?

indicators.note: a size label goes up from small to large, so the small letter is swapped for the large one

parts.note: the setter speaking: what a crossword setter does is setting the puzzle

explanation.surface: A puzzled grower asks what they are up to, allowing something to get bigger.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'I' is the setter, so 'What am I doing' gives SETTING. Clothing sizes run S (small) to L (large): 'increase in size' turns S into L.
explanation.definitionFit: Letting someone do something is allowing it, so the participle matches 'permitting' as a synonym.

clue.text: Increases confusion involving the very rich

parts.note: Elon Musk, among the world's richest people
a '-gate' is a scandal, the sort of uproar named after Watergate; plural here

explanation.surface: A claim that inequality muddles things when billionaires are around.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as ELON + GATES: '-gates' are scandals that cause uproar, named after Watergate, and Elon Musk stands for the very rich. Bill Gates hovers behind the second half too.
explanation.definitionFit: To elongate is to lengthen, so 'elongates' is a synonym of 'increases' in the sense of making longer.

clue.text: Mate with sweetheart in bar — it's been arranged beforehand

indicators.note: something placed in a space sits within it, so one piece wraps around the others

parts.note: a pub is a bar
to tup is to mate, of a ram
jo is a Scots word for a sweetheart

explanation.surface: A man meets his girlfriend in a pub, and it's clearly a planned set-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mate' looks like a friend but is the verb used of rams. Jo is the Scots word from Burns's 'John Anderson, my jo'.
explanation.definitionFit: A put-up job is a scheme rigged in advance to deceive, so the clue's clause describes such a staged affair.

clue.text: Again put down Romeo's iconic car

parts.note: Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the Jaguar E-type, a classic British sports car

explanation.surface: Romeo's classic car has been knocked down again, or put down once more.
explanation.walkthrough: The Jaguar E-type is the 1960s British sports car often called the most beautiful ever made. 'Put down' here means set down in writing.
explanation.definitionFit: To put words down is to record them, and keying them in a second time is entering them anew on a keyboard.

clue.text: Balls left by top seed — and racket

indicators.note: one person leaving another departs from them, so these letters drop out

parts.note: the top seed in a tournament is the number one seed, written NO 1 SEED
Ed Balls, the former Labour minister and TV personality

explanation.surface: A tennis match where balls are left behind by the leading player amid a lot of din.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' and 'racket' look like tennis kit; Balls is Ed Balls, the British politician, and 'racket' is the definition. NO 1 SEED with ED leaving gives NO 1 SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a loud, unpleasant din, which is a common synonym for a disturbing clamour of sound.

clue.text: Horny individual in college with my name

parts.note: uni is short for university
cor is an exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A randy student is at university bearing the speaker's own name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horny' looks like lust, but means having a horn. Cor is a British exclamation of surprise, so it can stand for 'my!'.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical beast is famous for the single spiral horn on its forehead, making it literally a creature with a horn.

clue.text: One visiting London's North, South, East and West (amongst others) in readiness for combat

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside the place being visited, so one piece is put within the other

parts.words: London's North, South, East and West (amongst others)
parts.note: North Acton, South Acton, East Acton and West Acton are all London Underground or Overground stations
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A tourist travels round every compass point of London, among other places, ready for a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass points are not N, S, E, W here: Acton in west London has stations prefixed by all four, so they are Acton stations.
explanation.definitionFit: Action stations is the military order for crews to take battle positions, so it describes being prepared to fight.

clue.text: Getting back in time, keep at it inside

indicators.note: to be inside something is to be enclosed by it, so one piece goes within another
going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters are read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written
a keep is a castle's stronghold, so a fort
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone travelling back in time is urged to keep going and persevere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' does double duty, completing the definition and turning 'at it' round. 'Keep' is the noun for a castle tower, not the verb it pretends to be.
explanation.definitionFit: Tit for tat is retaliation in kind, and getting back at someone means taking revenge on them for a wrong.

clue.text: One purple heart taken affecting pelvic area

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: when a word's heart is taken away its central letter is removed

parts.note: lilac is a pale purple

explanation.surface: A medical report on a purple heart drug that turns out to affect the hips.
explanation.walkthrough: Purple Heart sounds like the medal or the old amphetamine pill, but the heart is only the middle letter of a purple word.
explanation.definitionFit: Iliac is the anatomical adjective for the ilium, the broad upper hip bone, so it relates to the pelvis.

clue.text: Watching what vandal's doing to car which won't start

indicators.note: something that will not start has no beginning, so the first letter is lost

parts.note: vandals scratch car paintwork with a key, called keying

explanation.surface: A witness watches a vandal damaging a car that has broken down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Won't start' fits a dodgy car engine, but it tells you to drop the opening letter of the vandal's act.
explanation.definitionFit: To eye something is to look at it closely, so the participle is a synonym of looking or observing.

clue.text: Go for a working dinner, only the second offering meat

parts.note: go and pep both mean energy
per means for each, as in 'a pound a head'
a machine that is on is working

indicators.note: keeping only the second of something means just the letter in position two survives

parts.note: the second letter of the word

explanation.surface: An invitation to a business dinner where only the main course features meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' is a noun meaning energy, not a verb. 'Second' looks like the second course but picks out one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Pepperoni is a spicy Italian-American dried sausage, so it is one kind of cured meat, often found on pizzas.

clue.text: Begging Iran and Togo to settle

indicators.note: to settle a dispute is to sort things out, so the letters are sorted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A diplomatic appeal urging two countries to resolve their differences.
explanation.walkthrough: The country names are pure fodder. Rogation is a churchy word, best known from Rogation Sunday, when prayers of supplication are said.
explanation.definitionFit: Rogation comes from Latin rogare, to ask, and means solemn supplication or entreaty, a formal kind of pleading.

clue.text: Clergyman heard shot at table

indicators.note: what is heard is taken in by the ear, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: a canon is a member of a cathedral's clergy

explanation.surface: A priest overheard at dinner is shot at the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot at table' suggests a murder at dinner, but the table is a billiard or snooker table.
explanation.definitionFit: In billiards a cannon is a stroke in which the cue ball strikes two other balls in succession.

clue.text: Culture represented by apple pie, baseball, roots music and er- a maniac maybe?

definitions.text: Culture represented by apple pie, baseball, roots music

indicators.note: maybe signals one possible version, so the letters may be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A list of all-American things, ending with a hesitant suggestion that a madman belongs there too.
explanation.walkthrough: The hesitant 'er-' looks like filler but supplies two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Americana is the collective term for objects and traditions typical of the United States, such as its food, sport and folk music.

clue.text: Criticises GP over accepting 50 and change in conditions

indicators.note: accepting means taking something inside
over in a down clue means turned upside down, so the pair reads backwards

parts.note: to pan a show is to criticise it
a GP, general practitioner, is a doctor
L is the Roman numeral for 50

explanation.surface: Someone attacks their GP for taking a bribe of fifty, plus some loose change.
explanation.walkthrough: '50 and change' reads like money; 'change' belongs to the definition, a sudden turn in the weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold snap is a sudden short spell of cold weather, a change in weather conditions.

clue.text: Done so badly, it's lumpy

indicators.note: a job performed poorly comes out wrong, so the letters end up in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook's sauce or custard has been made so poorly that it's full of lumps.
explanation.walkthrough: Nodose is a botanical and medical word from Latin nodus, a knot.
explanation.definitionFit: Nodose means having nodes or knobbly swellings, so it describes something knotty, bumpy and uneven.

clue.text: Selectively read point I'd made

indicators.note: something made is built from raw material, so these letters are formed into a new word

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone accuses a reader of cherry-picking the argument they put forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Read' looks like a past tense, but the definition is an infinitive phrase: to read bits here and there.
explanation.definitionFit: To dip into a book is to sample parts of it casually instead of going through it from start to finish.

clue.text: Not all right, scenery in one part of England

parts.note: some means a part rather than all
R is the abbreviation for right
a stage set is theatre scenery

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the landscape in a part of England isn't quite right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scenery' suggests countryside but means a stage set. Somerset is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset is an English county in the West Country, so it is one of the administrative regions of England.

clue.text: Is being sent back — like that bloke maintained it's not cooked

indicators.note: held up or supported on both sides, so the following pieces sit inside
something sent back is returned the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: as means like, in the same way
him refers to a man already mentioned

explanation.surface: A diner complains a dish is being returned because a man claimed it was raw.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'like' as a word meaning the same, and 'that bloke' as a pronoun; both sit inside the backwards 'Is'. The definition is a description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Sashimi is Japanese thinly sliced raw fish, served without any cooking at all.

clue.text: Make a mistake transitioning and come clean

indicators.note: changing gender, here from male to female, so the male letter becomes the female one

parts.note: to mess up is to blunder

explanation.surface: Someone errs during a transition and then owns up.
explanation.walkthrough: M and F are the standard abbreviations for male and female; 'transitioning' swaps the M of MESS UP for an F.
explanation.definitionFit: To fess up is informal for confessing, which is the idiom of coming clean about something.

clue.text: Pick up contents of nappy by river! To what purpose?

indicators.note: the contents of a container sit inside its walls, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters
R is the abbreviation for river
eh? is a way of saying what?
an end is an aim or purpose

explanation.surface: A parent by a riverbank, picking up a dirty nappy, wonders why they bother.
explanation.walkthrough: A nappy is a baby's diaper. 'Pick up' sounds like collecting litter but means arresting someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Police apprehend a suspect when they arrest them, and pick up is a colloquial term for such an arrest.

clue.text: Councillor never showing up to register

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top
what is showing is visible on the surface, so the letters are there in the words

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A councillor who never turns up to sign on for duties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Showing up' reads as attendance, but splits into two jobs: showing the letters, then sending them up the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol is to sign up officially for a course or list, which makes it a synonym of putting your name down.

clue.text: One son in clear — it's not the full picture

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: a thing placed in another sits within it, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: a net sum is what is clear after deductions
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A son has been cleared of something, but there is more to the story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear' looks like an acquittal but means to earn after deductions, so net.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is a small picture set inside a larger one, such as a detail map, so it shows only part of the scene.

clue.text: Bashir's odds slashed? Mental!

indicators.note: slashing something cuts part of it away, so these letters are removed

parts.note: Shoaib Bashir is an England cricketer who bowls off-spin
SP is the starting price, the betting odds at the start of a race

explanation.surface: A bookmaker cuts the odds on Bashir, and a punter thinks that is crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mental' looks like slang for mad but means of the mind. SP, starting price, is the British betting abbreviation for the odds when a race begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Inner can describe the private life of the mind and emotions, as in inner thoughts, so it fits psychological.

clue.text: An elite fighter shortly entering very small country

indicators.note: entering means going in, so the article and the shortened fighter go inside the word for very

parts.note: so means very, as in 'so kind'

indicators.note: shortly here means made short, so the fighter's word loses its last letter

parts.note: a marine is a soldier of an elite seaborne force

explanation.surface: A commando briefly slips into a tiny nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very' seems to qualify 'small', making 'very small country' the definition, but it is the container the other pieces are 'entering'; only 'small country' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: San Marino, an enclave inside Italy, is one of the world's tiniest independent states.

clue.text: Idle, so I applied to perform with those I might come across

parts.note: to loll is to laze about

indicators.note: to perform is to act something out, so the letters are put to work in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lazy jobseeker applies to work with people they might bump into.
explanation.walkthrough: Lollipop ladies are British school crossing patrol wardens, named after their round stop signs. 'Come across' looks like meeting by chance, but means crossing the road with their help.
explanation.definitionFit: The patrol wardens escort children over busy roads, so they are the people a child crosses the street with.
